div.p: Power consumption is a major design issue in modern microprocessors. Hence, power reduction techniques, like Dynamic Voltage Scaling (DVS), are being widely implemented. Unfortunately, they impact on the task execution time so difficulting schedulability of hard real-time applications.

To deal with this problem, this paper proposes a poweraware scheduler for coarse-grain embedded multicore processors implementing global DVS. To this end, this work presents two heuristics, namely Balanced Memory and Balanced CPU, which distribute the task set among cores focusing on resource utilization.
Results show that with respect to a system not implementing DVS, two or five DVS levels achieve energy savings by about 35% or 51%, respectively.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In the last years, the problem of power consumption has been a major concern in current high-performance microprocessor design, at both scopes, either singlecore and multicore architectures. Many of these systems implement multithreading capabilities to increase their performance level.

Three main multithreading models have been devised [1]: simultaneous, coarse-grain, and fine-grain multithreading. Processors implementing the former model are the most complex and power hungry because of the issue logic, so making it unpredictable, while the latter model sacrifices single-thread performance for overall throughput so priority schemes cannot be supported. Unlike simultaneous multithreading, coarsegrain processors issue only instructions from one thread at a given cycle and are able to switch the running thread when a long latency event occurs (e.g., a main memory access). In such a case, both the core and memory work simultaneously, and this time is referred to as overlapping time. Because of these reasons, the coarse-grain model is the best choice to trade off power to performance. Nowadays, multicore/multithreaded processors are being implemented in a wide scope of computers. In this context, an important growing segment of the market is filled with embedded systems which require a high number of cores to deal with the features that they control. Furthermore, when these processors are used in critical embedded real-time applications, power consumption must be specially tackled because of the battery lifetime constraints.

Many techniques have been proposed to deal with power consumption. A widely implemented technique applying on the entire system in multicore/multithreaded processors is Dynamic Voltage Scaling (DVS) [2]. For instance, the Transmeta Crusoe and the Intel Xeon make use of DVS. This mechanism allows the system to work at different voltage/frequency levels. The lower the selected level the higher the execution time but also the higher the power savings. DVS can be classified as local DVS or global DVS. It has been shown [3] that if the load is fairly balanced, global DVS can be as efficient as local DVS.

When implementing DVS in real-time systems, it may happen that slowing down the processor speed (to save energy) leads to situations where the schedulability of the system cannot be guaranteed. Moreover, this situation becomes a main concern for hard realtime systems where deadlines misses are not permitted. Therefore, the scheduler must be designed aimed at minimizing the energy consumption while guaranteeing the task deadline [4], [5], [6]. In processors implementing DVS, this means that the processor speed should be adapted to fullfil the deadline constraints of the tasks. If this job is performed by the scheduler (as assumed in this work), then the scheduler must select not only the new task to be run but also the lowest DVS level fulfilling the hard real-time constraints. In a multicore system this problem exarcebates, since the overall workload must be previously balanced among cores, according to a given criterion or partitioning heuristic [7], in order to efficiently run the programs.

This paper has two main contributions.First, we propose a hard real-time power-aware scheduling system for a coarse-grain embedded multicore processor working with global DVS, which reduces the power consumption while guaranteeing schedulability. Second, we analyze how the overlapping time of corunning tasks, by designing partitioning heuristics, can help to improve energy savings across three different frequency/voltage models.

The remaining of this paper is structured as follows. Section II discusses the related work. Section III presents the proposal. Section IV analyzes the experimental results. Finally, Section V presents some concluding remarks.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Some research studies have addressed the problem of energy management in multiprocessor platforms when scheduling real-time tasks [8], [4], [5]. In multiprocessors platforms, where this problem is NP-hard [2], two main scheduling approaches can be found attending to wether global or partitioned scheduling is applied. In global scheduling [8], a task is placed in a queue of executable tasks that is shared among all processors in the system from where the highest priority executable tasks are selected for execution on the available processors. In such model, tasks are allowed to migrate among processors. As opposite, in partitioned scheduling [4], [5], a task is assigned permanently to a given processor and it is not allowed to migrate. This technique splits the multiprocessor scheduling problem to many uniprocessors, allowing well established algorithms (e.g., EDF (Earliest Deadline First) [9]) from uniprocessor theory to be adopted. In [8], Aydin and Yang address the problem of reducing energy for periodic real-time tasks in symmetric multiprocessor platforms (SMP) using DVS. To this end, the EDF algorithm is used to analyze the effect of partitioning heuristics. In [4], Al Enawy and Aydin consider the problem of energy minimization for periodic preemptive hard real-time tasks scheduled on a SMP with DVS capability. They use partitioned scheduling and assume that static RMS priorities are assigned to tasks. In [5], Anderson and Baruah deal with the system synthesis problem of periodic realtime tasks on identical multiprocessors by using EDF global scheduling. These works do not consider the sharing of resources, which has a strong impact on reducing energy in multithreaded systems, such as the memory-processor overlapping tackled in this paper.

Other researches have focused on multithreaded processors.In [10] Cazorla et al. present an architecture where a SMT (simultaneous multithreading processor) interacts with the operating system to improve performance. However, the problem of combining energy management with the schedulability guarantee is not resolved. Moreover, in [11], El-Haj-Mahmoud et al. state that SMT processors difficult proving hard-realtime guarantees, and propose a virtual in-order superscalar architecture which virtualizes a superscalar architecture in various processors. This architecture incorporates a static scheduler to execute periodic tasks. They compare their scheduler to an EDF for multiprocessors in terms of rate of deadline misses.

Regarding computation/memory overlap among real-time tasks, El-Haj-Mahmoud and Rotenberg [12] devise a technique that provides a coarse-grain multithreaded processor the capability to tolerate memory latencies in hard real-time systems. They derive a closed-form schedulability test to determine whether a hard real-time task set is schedulable in the context of weighted-round-robin scheduling on a multithreaded processor.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL AND POWER-AWARE SCHEDULING
A. System model and task set
div.p: The modeled system, shown in Figure 1, consists of a bi-core processor, a partitioner, a power-aware scheduling system, and the source and sink of periodic real-time tasks. Each one is a coarse-grain multithreaded processor. Although the study can be generalized for m cores, two cores have been assumed for evaluation purposes. Both cores model an ARM11 MP-processor [13] based processor implementing three hardware threads and sharing a global DVS regulator. The partitioning heuristics distribute ready tasks among the EDF schedulers and try to improve the feasibility and power consumption of the system by balancing the workload. The EDF based scheduler executes the tasks from the head of its ordered queue, that is, the task with the earliest deadline has the highest priority. Each scheduler writes an input/output port which is always being read by the DVS. Notice that only the partitioner is aware of the tasks location and both schedulers work independently from each other. In this way, the scheduling process is significantly simplified with respect to a global scheduler. Finally, the DVS hardware adjusts the frequency of the system according to the schedulers requirements.

The task set consists of n periodical real-time tasks, T = {T 1 , ..., T n }. Each task T i is characterized by three main parameters, T i = {W CET i , P i , D i }. The W CET refers to the Worst Case Execution Time, and is a prerequisite for real time applications [14]. It can be either measured in the real system or estimated in an analytical way. In this work, the W CET i was obtained by running the task i at the lowest processor frequency. This time was split in two main components attending to the resources that the task consumes, (i.e., processor and memory). Therefore, task characterization remains as T i = {W CET i (cpu i , m i ), P i , D i }. P i is the task period, that is, the time at which T i restarts execution. Finally, D i refers to the task deadline which is the time allowed to complete a task. To simplify task scheduling, EDF implementations usually assume that task deadlines match their periods [8], as also done in this paper (P i = D i ). Tasks arrive to the system dynamically from the source -the number of tasks varies according to mode changes in real-time applications [15]-, execute a given number of periods (active), log off the system, and go to the sink.

div.head: B. Partitioning heuristics
div.p: As coarse grain multithreaded processors switch processor control among threads each time a long latency event occurs (e.g., a L2 cache miss), the memory activity of a given thread can overlap with the processor activity of another thread so delivering a slack time to the scheduling system. Therefore, the higher the overlapping time the higher the potential energy savings. Notice that a high overlapping ratio can be reached when co-running threads are complementary regarding processor and memory resource requirements.

To evaluate the energy savings provided by the power-aware scheduling system, two partitioning heuristics were devised namely BM (Balanced Memory) and BC (Balanced CPU). These heuristics distribute memory and processor requirements, respectively, in a balanced way (i.e., as close as possible to fifty-fifty) among both cores. In this way, both heuristics act as a catalyst to increase the overlapping time between memory and CPU. In addition, to evaluate how these heuristics perform, an unbalanced heuristic namely UR (Unbalanced Resources) was also modeled.

Depending on the time that the tasks reach the system, they can be delivered to the cores in two different ways: i) the initial set of tasks is delivered according to the proposed heuristics, ii) when a new task arrives to the system, the partitioner allocates it in the less loaded core. The last, referred to as Worst Fit [4], pursues to balance the system workload. As a consequence, when a new task arrives, the system could not require to turn up the frequency level to fulfill the real-time constraints.

div.head: C. Power-aware scheduling system
div.p: The power-aware scheduling system is composed of EDF based schedulers and the DVS mechanism. In this proposal, the EDF behavior performs two main functions. First, the task queue in each core always keeps sorted according to the normal EDF algorithm, that is, tasks are properly allocated when they arrive to the queue. Second, a ready task can execute as soon as it reaches the queue head provided that there is a free hardware thread context in the core. If no thread context is available but a lower priority task is running, preemption is applied.

To deal with power consumption, the EDF based scheduler must cooperate with the DVS mechanism. The former, selects the lowest frequency F i at which the system is schedulable and provides this value to the DVS hardware. The latter, chooses the maximum frequency between the ones received from both schedulers, and supplies these values (frequency and voltage) to both cores .

The scheduler selects the lowest frequency each time the task set changes, that is, each time a task arrives to or leaves the system. This is done because of two main reasons: i) as the workload has changed, a different frequency (lower or higher) could be more appropriate, and ii) it may happen that because of a good overlapping, the tasks already running in the core get a slack time that allows the scheduler to fulfill realtime constraints at a lower frequency. To drive dynamic changes in the frequency, the scheduler runs the EDF test for the new frequency and changes it in case of the system is schedulable.

div.head: IV. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
div.p: The power-aware scheduling system has been evaluated on top of the detailed cycle-by-cycle multithreaded multicore Multi2Sim simulation framework [16], which was extended to implement the real-time schedulers, the frequency models, and to deal with hard real-time tasks.

div.head: A. Designing and planning mixes execution
div.p: A wide set of benchmarks from the Real-Time Systems Benchmark repository [17] has been used to carry out the experiments. Using these benchmarks, a set of mixes has been designed to explore the potential energy savings. To this end, we followed a methodology consisting of four main steps: i) benchmark characterization, ii) benchmark classification, iii) mix composition, and iv) mix execution planning.

The benchmarks used through the experiments have been classified attending to their processor and memory consumption. For each resource, benchmarks are classified in three main groups depending on if they have few, high, or intermediate resource requirements. Once the benchmarks have been classified, heterogeneous mixes can be straightforwardly designed by choosing benchmarks belonging to different groups. After that, mixes ares are partitioned between cores according to a given partition heuristic (see Section III-B). Each heuristic will provide a given distribution of memory and CPU activities for each core.

Finally, in the last step, the execution of the mix is planned out. The reason behind this step is that in critical real-time control applications, real-time tasks are dynamically entering and leaving the system at different rates (mode changes). Therefore, to evaluate these systems we need to select which benchmarks belong to each mix and also how these benchmarks behave along the mix hyperperiod (lowest common multiple of the benchmarks period).

div.head: B. Estimating Energy Savings
div.p: The power-aware scheduling system works for any range of frequency/voltage levels, thus, energy benefits depend on how wide is the range and the number of levels supported by the DVS regulator. This work evaluates the proposed scheduling system working with different models of frequency/voltage. Three models have been evaluated supporting 2, 3, and 5 frequency/voltage levels, and referred to as 2L, 3L, and 5L, respectively. The 5L model allows all the five frequencies (100Mhz, 200Mhz, 300Mhz, 400Mhz, and 500Mhz), and the 2L model only works with the extreme frequencies. Finally, the 3L also supports the intermediate one. Frequency/voltage and energy values were chosen resembling the ones of the Pentium M microprocessor [18].

In addition, for comparison purposes, two different models have been also evaluated: a baseline model and a naive two-level (2LN) frequency scheduling system. The baseline assumes that the processor always works at its maximum speed. The 2LN scheduler assumes that the system always works at its maximum speed except when there is no task executing in any core. At that point, the frequency is down to the lowest one until any task in the system restars its execution. In such a case, the system speed is restored to the previous one (the maximum in the 2LN model). This enhancement has been also implemented in the rest of models.

The total energy consumption was obtained running each mix for each heuristic along its hyperperiod. For each case, the elapsed time that the processor runs at each frequency/voltage level was measured and the accumulated energy was obtained by multiplying these values by the energy that each level consumes per cycle.

Figure 2 plots the energy consumption relative to the baseline model. That is, energy values have been normalized to the energy consumed by a processor working at its maximum frequency (energy equals to 1). Power benefits can be straightforwardly deduced. For instance, a value of 0.45 means that a given heuristic requires 45% the energy savings required by the baseline, that is, the heuristic achieves energy savings by 55% (i.e., 1 -0.45). From the graphics shown in this figure, three main conclusions can be drawn.

Regarding the partitioning heuristics, BM (see Figure 2(a)) is the heuristic having the lowest average normalized power consumption, by about 10% (i.e., 0.59 -0.49) less than the unbalanced heuristic for the 5L model, which supposes about 21% relative energy savings. This is because the memory time is significantly higher than the processor time (about four times, on average). Therefore, the overlapping time highly increases when the memory requirements are balanced, so allowing the scheduling system to turn down the speed more than the BC heuristic.

Regardless the applied heuristic, the best results are obtained when working with a higher number of frequency/voltage levels. This is because when the system has a wide range of frequencies, there are more opportunities to find one frequency that fits better the system requirements.

Energy differences among the 2L and the 2LN levels are not significant (about 4%, on average, when using the BM heuristic). The reason is because the 2L model has not many chances to change frequency/voltage levels each time that it applies, as mentioned above. However, even in this case the BM heuristic provides energy benefits up to 24% (see Figure 2 Finally, the main conclusion that can be drawn is that by using the power-aware scheduling system with a high number of frequency levels (5L) and a fair heuristic strategy (BM or BC), power benefits are by 40% higher than using a 2LN model using no heuristic whatsoever.

V. CONCLUSIONS Two balancing heuristics (BM and BC) have been used to evaluate the power-aware scheduling proposal. This heuristics partition the real-time tasks among the cores in order to further reduce the energy consumption of the system. As expected, the heuristics have a strong impact on the power consumption. Experimental results show that BM is the best heuristic and, for five frequency/voltage levels, provides around 21% more energy savings with respect to applying no heuristic (UR). Also, for the same heuristic, it is shown that the number of frequency/voltage levels implemented also affects the energy. For instance, the energy savings achieved with 5 levels improve, on average, about 32% with respect to a 2-level system. Finally a system having a single frequency/voltage level would consume about 2.08 times the energy consumed by the system implementing the BM heuristic with a wide range of frequency levels (5L).
